Chapter 7: Adapting Roles and Skills—Navigating Change with Confidence
As artificial intelligence becomes a bigger part of our daily work, you might notice your own role—along with the skills you need—begin to shift.
Sure, that change can feel a bit uncertain at first. But what if you looked at it as an open door? It’s actually a great chance for both growth and reinvention.
The trick is to meet these changes with curiosity and a sense of agency, not fear.
So, how do you move forward with confidence as everything starts to evolve?
Start by focusing on skills that make you a great partner for AI, instead of seeing it as competition. Let’s talk about a few of those:
First, there’s prompt design. This means learning how to give AI clear, effective instructions—almost like getting better at asking the right questions in a conversation.
Next, critical review. Here, your job is to look over what AI produces, refine it, and make sure it’s accurate and truly useful.
Then, there’s collaboration—working as a team where both people and AI bring their strengths to the table.
And finally, ethical reasoning. That’s about thinking ahead and considering the wider impact of decisions powered by AI.
What’s interesting is these aren’t just technical skills—they’re deeply human ones.
Take prompt design, for example. Mastering it is a lot like learning to ask great questions when you’re talking to someone. You need to be clear, specific, and aware of what the other person—or the AI—can actually do.
Now, you might wonder—how do organizations fit into all this?
They can really help by offering training, encouraging people to experiment, and celebrating new forms of expertise.
But you don’t have to wait for someone else to take the lead. You can own your growth by finding learning resources, practicing new skills, and sharing what you discover with your peers.
I like to think of this whole period as a kind of skills garden. Some old plants—or skills—might need a little trimming, while new ones are just starting to grow.
The garden really thrives when you keep tending to it, noticing what’s growing well and what could use a bit more care.
So, yes—change can feel a bit unsettling. But it’s also a powerful moment to rediscover your strengths, build brand new capabilities, and help shape the future of work in ways that matter to you.
